e.t: Abennēr, also rendered Avennir, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a man in the Old Testament narrative. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 59 times, most often in 2 Samuel, where repeated references distinguish this individual from other people in the story. Its meaning as a name should therefore be understood through the person it identifies and the surrounding passage, rather than treated as a general vocabulary term.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Adōnikam” or “Athonikam.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezra: 2:13 and 8:13. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific role in each list cannot be described further, but its basic function is clear: it is the name of an individual.

Ἀθηναῖος is a proper name referring to an Athenian, someone associated with Athens. It functions as a personal or identifying name rather than as a description of an action, feeling, or moral quality. The gloss preserves the name as “Athēnaios” or “Athineos.” In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: in 2 Maccabees 6:1 and 9:15. Those references identify where the word appears, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its particular role in either passage.

This adjective describes something morally disgraceful, dirty, or shameful. It can characterize a person, action, or condition that deserves dishonor rather than respect. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times, so its basic sense is consistent even though the surrounding context determines exactly what is being judged. The word is used in Genesis and in later Jewish writings, including Wisdom and Maccabees. Its central idea remains that of something contemptible or dishonorable.

This adjective means “unburnt”: something that has not been consumed, scorched, or changed by fire. It describes the condition of an object or material, rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 20:26. The word’s basic sense remains focused on being untouched by burning; the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there. Its lexical meaning is explicitly given as “unburnt.”

This adjective describes someone who belongs to a different family or group from the one being discussed. It marks a distinction of family or belonging, identifying a person as an outsider to the particular household, lineage, or community in view. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 34 times, so it is used across several passages rather than for only one specific situation. Its exact force in a verse depends on which family or group the surrounding context sets apart.

This word is the proper name Haman, also rendered Aman, a person named throughout the Greek Old Testament book of Esther. It identifies the same individual across the narrative rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, the name occurs 54 times, appearing from Esther 1:1 through Esther 10:3. The precise significance of each mention comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions simply as a personal name.

This Greek LXX verb means “take up” or “take along.” It describes lifting something or taking a person or thing with you, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 82 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is used broadly rather than being limited to one setting. Its exact sense in a particular verse depends on what is being taken up or carried along in the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “obstinate.” It describes a person who persists stubbornly rather than yielding. As a verb, it expresses the act or condition of being obstinate, not merely a fixed personal label. It occurs 49 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it is used across a range of scriptural passages to describe persistent resistance or stubborn conduct. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “pack”: it describes the action of putting things together for carrying or transport. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 14:36. The surrounding verse is needed to determine the precise situation in which the packing takes place, but the word itself plainly points to gathering and preparing belongings for movement.

Arbēla, also rendered Arvila, is a proper name for a place rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Numbers 34:11. Because it is a place name, its meaning is primarily its identification of a geographic location; the supplied lexical information does not provide an additional ordinary definition or explain the location’s features.

This adjective describes something that is acceptable or accommodating—something regarded as pleasing or suitable. It can describe a person, action, choice, or arrangement that meets an expectation or is received favorably. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 26 times, so its basic sense is used across a range of situations rather than belonging to only one setting. The surrounding verse determines what is considered acceptable in each occurrence.

Ariph, also rendered Arif, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or family name in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs twice in the Greek text of Nehemiah, at Nehemiah 7:24 and Nehemiah 10:20. Since no wider lexical definition is given, its meaning is its function as a personal designation, while the surrounding passage identifies whom the name refers to in each occurrence.

This is a proper name referring to a person named “Asaēl,” also identified as “Asel.” It functions as a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 17 times across 16 verses, with occurrences from 2 Samuel through Ezra. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding account, but the lexical information identifies it as the name of a person.

Asena is a proper name, referring to a person named Asena. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Ezra 2:50. The available wording preserves the name itself rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. Therefore, its ordinary meaning is simply the personal name Asena; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s particular role in that passage.

Asoube, also rendered Asuve, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not presented here as a word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship, so its lexical role is simply to name someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 3:20. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the person’s family connection or place in that genealogy cannot be described further from this word alone.

Asphar, also given as Asfar, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity, but the available lexical information does not establish whether that entity is a person, place, or something else. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Maccabees 9:33. No broader lexical sense is established for it.

This word describes someone as an “absolute master of”—one possessing complete authority over what follows. It can function as an adjective or noun, so it may characterize a person or identify that person by this position of supreme mastery. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any sentence depends on the surrounding words.

This is a proper name for a Baithleemite, or Vethleemitis—someone identified by association with Bethlehem. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 2 Samuel 21:19. The word functions as a personal designation rather than a general description of an action, quality, or object. Its single occurrence means its precise role in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, but the name itself marks Bethlehem-related identity.

This adverb describes an action done heavily or fiercely, emphasizing unusual force or intensity. It tells the reader how something happens rather than naming a person, thing, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense points to an action carried out with great weight, severity, or fierceness.

Belasōr, also rendered Velasor, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 2 Samuel 13:23, identifying a person or named individual in the passage. Because it is a name, its meaning is chiefly its identification of that individual, not a general concept that can be applied elsewhere. The name itself does not provide further description without the surrounding verse text.

This Greek LXX noun means “letter-carrier,” referring to a person who carries or delivers written messages. It names a messenger whose particular duty is transporting letters, rather than describing the letter itself or the message’s content. The word occurs twice in the Greek text of Esther, in Esther 3:13 and Esther 8:10. Its ordinary meaning remains focused on the person performing this task; the surrounding verse determines the specific assignment or circumstances involved.

“Galaad” or “Galaath” is a proper name, not a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it functions as the name of a specific biblical individual, place, or people-group designation rather than expressing a quality shared by many things. It appears 122 times in the LXX corpus, from Genesis through Song of Songs, with most occurrences in the Old Testament books. The exact referent in a particular verse depends on its surrounding passage.

Goudiēl, also rendered Guthil, is a proper name referring to a person rather than a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs twice, both times in Numbers 13:10 and Numbers 13:15. Since no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the name itself identifies the person, while the passage supplies the specific role or significance attached to him.

This Greek LXX verb means “turn by entreaty”: it describes changing someone’s direction or response through pleading or earnest request. The emphasis is on influence achieved by an appeal rather than by force. It appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 2:17. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic sense is to turn or redirect through entreaty.

This word means “grievously,” describing something done or experienced with severe pain, distress, or seriousness. As an adverb, it tells how an action or condition occurs rather than naming a person or thing. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, in two separate deuterocanonical verses. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense is clear: something happens in a deeply troubling or painful manner.

This is a proper name rendered “Ezraΐtēs” or “Ezretis.” It functions as a personal designation rather than an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 5:11. The available lexical information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whom it identifies or what role that person has in the passage. Its precise significance there therefore depends on the context of 1 Kings 5:11.

This Greek LXX verb means “faint” or “let loose.” It can describe someone becoming weak or losing strength, or something being released or allowed to go. The surrounding sentence determines which sense is intended. It occurs 42 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic idea appears in more than one kind of setting. It is not a noun or title, but an action word describing what someone does or what happens to someone.

Elkana is a personal name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a proper name, not as a general description, action, or quality. The name appears 17 times in 17 verses within the Greek Old Testament corpus, from Exodus through 2 Chronicles, with several occurrences in 1 Samuel and 1 Chronicles. Its precise reference depends on the person named in each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “blow in/on,” describing the act of directing breath or air toward something. It can refer simply to blowing, whether onto a person or object, rather than naming the result or purpose of the action. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including Genesis, Kings, Job, Ezekiel, Nahum, and Wisdom. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on what is being blown toward and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “contend”: to engage in a struggle or exert oneself in a serious contest. It describes active participation rather than passive concern, presenting a person as striving toward an outcome. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:16. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central sense remains purposeful, strenuous contending. It is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus rather than treated as a Greek New Testament entry.

This Greek verb means “pour out like rain.” It describes liquid or something else being released abundantly, with the image of rainfall coming down from above. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in Sirach, at Sirach 1:19 and Sirach 10:13. Its verbal form focuses on the action of pouring out rather than on the thing poured out. The surrounding verse determines whether the image is literal or serves as a comparison, but the central idea remains a plentiful outpouring.

This Greek LXX verb means “press down” or “weigh down.” It describes an action that bears heavily upon something or someone, emphasizing pressure or burden rather than merely touching or approaching. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related writings preserved in the LXX corpus, once in Daniel and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but its central idea remains the placing of weight or pressure upon something.

This Greek LXX verb means “give to” or “give in.” It describes handing something over, yielding, or submitting rather than holding back. The exact object or situation must come from the surrounding verse, but the word itself centers on transferring something to another person or yielding to a demand or circumstance. It occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across several kinds of passages. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality.

gl: have hospitable relations with; intimate with
d: have hospitable relations with; intimate with

e.t: This verb describes having hospitable relations with someone or becoming intimate with them. It refers to close personal association, especially the kind expressed through welcome and fellowship. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: in Esther, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is forming or maintaining a close relationship through hospitality or intimacy.

This verb means to contribute or supply something that is needed. It describes the act of providing or furnishing a share, resource, or help rather than merely possessing it. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 25:22. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense remains active provision: giving what is needed for a purpose or situation. It is therefore a practical word for supplying or contributing something useful.

This Greek LXX verb means to “question” or “request.” It describes speaking to someone to seek information, ask for something, or make an inquiry. The word is used broadly across the Greek Old Testament and related writings, appearing 64 times in this corpus. Its basic sense may point either to asking a question or to making a request, depending on the surrounding sentence. Because no verse text is provided here, the precise force in any particular passage must be determined from its context.

This verb means to deliver the good message or gospel, and therefore to preach. It describes communicating news presented as good and worth proclaiming, rather than merely speaking about an ordinary matter. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 22 times, showing a recurring action of announcing such a message. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding words and situation, but its central idea remains the public or personal delivery of good news.

Zechōra, also rendered Zekhora, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 36:5. The name identifies an individual in that passage, but the name itself does not express a broader concept or instruction. Its precise reference is established by the surrounding verse and passage, not by the name alone.

Zogor is a proper name rendered as “Zogor.” As a name, it identifies a particular person, place, or other named subject rather than expressing an ordinary quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Jeremiah 31:34. The surrounding verse text is not provided here, so the named subject cannot be identified more specifically. Its dependable meaning is simply the proper name “Zogor”; the passage determines what it refers to.

Tharsis is a proper name, referring to a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The English rendering preserves the name as “Tharsis,” so it is not translated into an ordinary descriptive meaning. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 22 times across 18 verses, from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its precise referent in any particular passage must be determined from that passage’s surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “heap,” referring to a gathered pile or mass of things. It occurs once in the Greek text represented here, in Sirach 20:28. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, the word’s specific reference in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning remains a heap: something collected or lying together in a mound or pile.

Iaous, also written Iaus, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here: once in 1 Chronicles 7:10 and once in 2 Chronicles 11:19. The available information identifies the name itself, but does not provide the surrounding verse text needed to explain the particular people or events connected with either occurrence.

Ieriēl, also rendered Ieril, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in 1 Chronicles 7:2 and once in 2 Chronicles 20:16. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular role in each passage cannot be described further, but its lexical function is simply to name a person.

Iesmega, also rendered Iezmega, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Samuel 27:10. Without the surrounding verse text, its exact referent cannot be stated more specifically, but its basic function is to distinguish that particular person or place from others.

Iōakim, also rendered Ioakim, is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 50 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, appearing especially in Jeremiah and 2 Kings. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on which person named Iōakim is being discussed.

This Greek LXX verb means “nail on”: to fasten something by driving a nail into it. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 118:120. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, which are not included here. Its central idea remains the physical act of securing something firmly with a nail.

Kainē, also rendered Keni, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named figure or designation, but the available information does not establish which specific referent is intended in every passage. The name occurs six times in the LXX, in 1 Samuel, Job, and Isaiah. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This noun refers to a tie or bandage—something used to bind or wrap. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 1:6. Its central idea is a binding strip or fastening rather than an action or abstract quality. The English rendering bandages agrees with this basic sense, while the precise force in Isaiah depends on the surrounding context. It describes a tangible object used for binding or covering.

This Greek LXX verb means to devise wickedly against someone—to plan or act with hostile, harmful intent. It describes purposeful opposition rather than a merely accidental act. As a verb, it expresses what someone does: forming a wicked scheme against another person or group. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 82:4, so its precise force there belongs to that passage’s surrounding context. Its direct meaning remains focused on deliberate, morally evil opposition.

This noun means “slander” or “calumny”: damaging speech or an accusation directed against another person. It names the act or charge itself rather than the person who speaks it. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 26:5. The word’s basic meaning is therefore focused and specific: speech that harms someone’s reputation. The surrounding verse is needed to explain how that idea functions in its particular setting.

This Greek LXX verb means “shut”: to close something so that an opening, entrance, or access is no longer open. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, where its ordinary sense remains the act of closing or keeping something closed. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being shut and the surrounding passage.

Koritē, also rendered Koriti, is a proper name rather than a descriptive word. It identifies a person in the Greek Septuagint and does not itself express an action, quality, or doctrine. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 9:31. Because the name appears only there and no surrounding verse text is provided here, its precise identity must be determined from that passage rather than from the name alone.

This Greek word means “roll.” It is a verb describing the act of moving something by turning it over and over, or causing something to move in that way. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs ten times, chiefly in passages translated from the Old Testament, with one occurrence in the deuterocanonical books. The basic idea remains simple and physical: something is rolled, or someone rolls it. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being moved and how the action functions in context.

This Greek LXX noun means “carousal”: a lively, festive gathering marked by revelry. It names the celebration or reveling itself rather than a person or object. The word occurs three times in the Greek deuterocanonical books, appearing once each in Wisdom, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains a carousal or festive revelry.

Lael, also given as Lel, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) and occurs once in that corpus, at Numbers 3:24. Because a personal name does not by itself state a person’s character or role, its specific significance must come from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This Greek LXX adjective means “flagstone,” referring to something made from or characterized by slabs of stone. It describes a stone-paved or flagstone-related feature rather than expressing an action, person, or feeling. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Chronicles, Esther, and Song of Songs. Its exact force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains a surface or feature associated with dressed stone or paving.

This Greek LXX verb means “grieve”: to experience or express deep sorrow. It describes the inward pain of distress and can also refer to the outward expression of that sorrow. The word occurs 44 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, showing that it is used across a broad range of passages involving loss, trouble, disappointment, or painful circumstances. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains sorrow that weighs on a person.

Manassēs, also rendered Manassis, is a proper name referring to Manasseh. It identifies a named person or the people and tribal line associated with that name in the Greek Old Testament. This is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs 152 times across 140 verses, especially in Joshua, Chronicles, and Numbers. The exact person or group intended depends on the surrounding passage.

gl: one who hates insolence; hater of insolence
d: one who hates insolence; hater of insolence

e.t: This noun means “one who hates insolence” or “hater of insolence.” It identifies a person whose disposition is opposed to insolence rather than describing the insolent person themselves. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 3 Maccabees 6:9. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on rejecting or opposing insolence.

This noun refers to “temple servants,” a group identified by their service connected with the temple. It names people rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. Its basic meaning remains focused on the people who served in this temple-related role; the precise duties or circumstances require the surrounding passage to explain.

Netōphati, also written Netofati, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or people associated with that name in the Old Testament Greek tradition. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Chronicles and Jeremiah. Its precise reference in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX noun refers to roaming about for pasture—the movement or condition of searching for grazing land. It can describe pasture-related wandering rather than a fixed place or settled activity. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including passages connected with animals, land, and people moving through grazing areas. Its exact emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains roaming in search of pasture.

This word means “ruin; destroy.” It is a verb describing an action that brings something to ruin or destruction, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Job. Its meaning remains consistent across these occurrences, while the surrounding verse determines what is being ruined or destroyed and the exact force of the action. It is therefore a relatively uncommon but clearly defined word in this corpus.

ὁμόνοια means “oneness of mind”: a condition in which people think together in agreement rather than being divided. As a noun, it names this shared unity of thought and purpose. Within this LXX corpus, it occurs seven times, describing a recognizable idea without being common throughout the collection. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains agreement and unity of mind.

This word means a hen. It is a noun naming the bird itself, rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears two times, both in 1 Kings. The word is found at 1 Kings 2:46 and 1 Kings 5:3, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain how the word functions in each passage. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it identifies a hen.

This word means “trap”: something set to catch, hold, or bring down a person or animal. As a noun, it can describe a literal device or, depending on the passage, a danger that ensnares someone. It occurs 60 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, showing that this is an established term for a trap or snare. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding wording and situation.

This Greek LXX verb means to send someone or something onward, or to convey it past a place or point. It describes movement away or beyond, rather than simply sending in a general sense. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, in Esther and 3 Maccabees. Its exact emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its central idea remains sending onward or passing something along.

This noun means “retraction; delay”: it refers either to pulling something back or to a postponement. Its basic idea is movement away from immediate completion or fulfillment, whether by withdrawal or by holding something back in time. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Job 25:3. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify its precise sense in context and determine whether the emphasis is withdrawal or postponement.

This adjective means “on foot,” describing people who travel or move by walking rather than by riding or using an animal or vehicle. It identifies the manner of movement, not a person’s character or status. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs 19 times, showing a recurring way to describe travel or an assembled group’s movement. Its exact force in a verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means to bind something around another thing or to bandage it. It describes the action of wrapping or fastening, especially in a way that encloses or supports what is being covered. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Job 12:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic action is clear: something is bound around, tied up, or treated with a bandage.

gl: line round a circular body; periphery
d: line round a circular body; periphery

e.t: “Periphery” means the line or boundary that runs around a circular body—the outer edge or circumference. This Greek LXX noun names the surrounding boundary rather than the central area. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, both times in Ecclesiastes. Its basic sense is concrete and spatial: something traced around the outside of a rounded form. The surrounding passage is needed to determine how the word functions in each occurrence, but its lexical idea remains the outer line or edge.

This adjective means “sideways,” describing something arranged or directed toward the side rather than straight ahead. It can identify the position or direction of an object, movement, or feature. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, the word occurs 18 times, showing a recurring use for describing lateral placement or direction. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and the thing being described.

This word means “fullness,” referring to something brought to a complete or abundant state. As a noun, it describes the condition of being full rather than the act of filling something. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears ten times across ten verses, including passages in Exodus, Deuteronomy, Psalms, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Sirach. Its precise emphasis can depend on what is being described—such as abundance, completion, or the full measure of something—but its central idea remains fullness or completeness.

This verb means to “live long” or “live many years.” It describes continued life over an extended period, focusing on longevity rather than a particular action or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 4:26, so its normal meaning is clear even though the available record does not include the verse’s surrounding text. The word functions as an action or condition attributed to people: they live for many years. [p03:word:lxx:L710651:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L710651:occurrences]

This Greek LXX verb means “play,” describing the action of engaging in play or behaving in a playful way. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here: once in Job and once in Sirach. The word’s basic sense remains centered on play rather than teaching, ruling, or working. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means “keep guard before” and describes guarding in advance or standing watch ahead of something. It functions as an action word, focusing on protective watchfulness rather than merely seeing or noticing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 22:24. Because it appears only once in this corpus and no verse text is provided here, its broader range cannot be established from repeated uses; its clear central idea is guarding beforehand.

ῥάσσω means “overthrow; dash,” describing forceful action that knocks something down or sends it forcefully against something. As a verb, it expresses decisive impact rather than a quiet movement or gradual change. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs six times, across six Old Testament verses in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Daniel. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is forceful striking, overthrow, or collapse.

Raphis, also rendered Rhafis, is a proper name in the Greek Septuagint. It identifies a specific named person or place rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 18:17. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not specify whether Raphis refers to a person or location, so that identification depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Roollam, also given as Rhoollam, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 11:19, so its lexical role is personal identification rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. No additional ordinary meaning is supplied for this name. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named there.

Sarich, also given as Sarikh, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise personal reference belongs to the passage where it appears, and no broader lexical meaning is provided here. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Samuel 22:5. The name should therefore be understood as identifying a person in that passage, without assigning it an unsupported symbolic or doctrinal meaning.
